outcome: Since 26 January 2024, exact minimum-energy configurations have been claimed for three individual values of n (7, 8 and 9), all posted in September and October 2026 and all Lean-based: N=8 as an arXiv preprint with Lean verification (18 Sep 2026), plus a second, Lean-based N=8 repository, N=7 as a vendor-posted Lean proof (27-28 Sep 2026), and N=9 as a single-author GitHub and Zenodo release (6 Oct 2026); the general question for all n is unchanged, and a 2024 heuristic paper reports an improved Coulomb energy at N=360 that I could not verify in the text.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one question indexed by n: (1) for each n points on the unit sphere S² in three-dimensional space, identify the configuration minimising the total Coulomb (1/r) repulsion energy, i.e. the sum over unordered pairs of 1/|xi - xj|, which is unique up to rotation and relabelling where it is unique; (2) the minimum energy value that configuration realises, for each n; (3) the bullet asks this for every n (its wording, 'what is the minimum energy configuration of n mutually-repelling particles', has no fixed n), so the all-n reading is that a general answer or method is wanted, and the single-n reading is that each instance is a question in its own right. The statement asserts no conjecture about which configuration is minimal, so it asks for the answer rather than asserting one. Reading note: the bullet does not name a formula, a conjectured polyhedron, or a bound.

events.what_happened: Richard Evan Schwartz posted 'The 5 Electron Case of Thomson's Problem' (arXiv:1001.3702, v1 21 Jan 2010), giving a rigorous computer-assisted proof that the triangular bipyramid is the unique configuration of 5 points on S² that globally minimises the Coulomb (1/r) energy. The abstract says 'We give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that'. Per Schwartz's own site, as reported in a search excerpt (not opened), it appeared in Experimental Mathematics 22(2), 2013, pp. 157-186. This event pre-dates the window and is recorded because it settles a case of the problem.
events.revisions: Journal version Experimental Mathematics 2013 per the author's site (search excerpt, journal page not opened). arXiv page shows v1 only.
events.delivers: Settles N=5 for the Coulomb case only: the triangular bipyramid is the unique global minimiser of the Coulomb energy for 5 points on S². Computer-assisted, with the code distributed by the author.
events.remains: Every other n, including N=7, N=8 and N=9, and the general all-n question.

events.directly_checkable: The triangular bipyramid is explicit (three equatorial points at 120 degrees and two poles); its Coulomb energy 6.474691495 (Wikipedia table) can be computed by hand from coordinates.
events.direction: Confirms the expected minimiser for N=5.
events.object: The triangular bipyramid (D3h) on 5 points, energy 6.474691495; explicit configuration. Optimality and uniqueness are established by a computer-assisted (rigorous) argument, not a non-constructive existence proof.

events.what_happened: Classical result reported only through secondary excerpts I read: Yudin's linear-programming method (in the Delsarte-Goethals-Seidel lineage) proves optimality of the regular tetrahedron, octahedron and icosahedron configurations for N=4, 6 and 12 points on S², for a class of energies that includes the Coulomb energy; the excerpt dates the method to 1992 ('first carried out for energy minimization by Yudin [Y92]'). I did not verify this in an opened source: the De Laat paper I opened (arXiv:1610.04905) does not mention Yudin, the Dragnev slides URL returned 404, and the Boyvalenkov-Dragnev-Hardin-Saff-Stoyanova paper (arXiv:1909.00981) does not contain the attribution.
events.delivers: Per secondary excerpts only: the Coulomb minimisers for N=4, 6 and 12 are proved optimal (N=2 and N=3 are elementary). Restricted to those N.
events.remains: All other N; per the excerpt, N=5 is not settled by this method.
events.directly_checkable: The tetrahedron, octahedron and icosahedron are explicit; their Coulomb energies (3.674234614, 9.985281374, 49.165253058) can be checked by hand.
events.doubts: Venue and exact year not confirmed in an opened source; the attribution rests on search excerpts of sources I did not open.
events.direction: Confirms the expected minimisers for N=4, 6, 12.
events.object: The regular tetrahedron (N=4), octahedron (N=6) and icosahedron (N=12); explicit configurations, optimality by a linear-programming (non-constructive, bound-based) argument per the excerpt.

events.what_happened: Schwartz posted 'The Phase Transition in 5 Point Energy Minimization' (arXiv:1610.03303, v1 11 Oct 2016), a computer-assisted monograph claiming that a computable constant S ≈ 15.048 exists such that the triangular bipyramid is the unique minimiser of the Riesz s-energy for 5 points for all s up to S. The abstract says 'This establishes the existence of the long-conjectured phase transition constant in 5-point energy minimization'. Later versions: 'Divide and Conquer: A Distributed Approach to Five Point Energy Minimization' (arXiv:2301.05090, Jan 2023), whose abstract says it proves the 1977 Melnyk-Knop-Smith phase-transition conjecture for 5 points, and a split into seven papers 'Five Point Energy Minimization 0-6' in April 2024 (per the author's site, via search excerpt, not opened). The author's site describes the claim as 'my (claimed) solution' and says the monograph is unpublished.
events.revisions: arXiv:2301.05090 (January 2023, updated and simplified version); seven-paper re-posting April 2024 per the author's site (not opened).
events.delivers: For N=5 only, and only for Riesz s-energies with s up to the phase-transition constant S ≈ 15.048. The Coulomb case (s=1) is a special value inside that range and was already settled for N=5 by the 2010 paper. Nothing about any N other than 5.
events.remains: All N other than 5; for N=5 nothing new for the Coulomb case; the Riesz phase-transition claim itself is unverified by any independent reader I found.
events.time_since_posted: 10 years since arXiv v1; no journal publication found
events.directly_checkable: Computer-assisted: the author states that code is available from his website; I did not download or run it.
events.doubts: The author's site says that attempts to publish the monograph have failed and that it 'still gives the impression of being too difficult to referee' (search excerpt of the site, not opened). I found no independent expert verification or published acceptance. The claim is about a power-law family, not the Coulomb problem for all n.
events.direction: Would be consistent with the Melnyk-Knop-Smith phase-transition conjecture for N=5; on the Thomson problem's own question it cuts in the expected direction only for N=5, which was already settled.
events.object: The triangular bipyramid for N=5 under Riesz s-energy with s below the constant S; the object is the same as in schwartz-2010-n5, with the claim extended over an interval of s by computer-assisted certificates.

events.what_happened: Moscato, Haque and Moscato, 'Continued fractions and the Thomson problem', Scientific Reports 13:7272, published 4 May 2023 (received 6 Sep 2022, accepted 18 Apr 2023). They fit analytic approximation formulas (continued fractions, found by symbolic regression and a memetic algorithm) to 453 putative optimal energies, up to n=4352, and report MSE 5.5549×10⁻⁸ for the normalised energy. The paper does not claim new minimal energies; its largest-case check uses the known value as reference. Pre-dates the window.
events.delivers: No exact result and no new minimal energy: an empirical formula for the minimal energy as a function of n, fitted to existing putative optima.
events.remains: Every exact minimiser for every n.
events.directly_checkable: The formula and the reference energies are in the paper; not checked by me.
events.doubts: Empirical fit, not a result about minima; it is included as a discounted event.
events.direction: No direction on exactness; it is consistent with the known putative minima.
events.object: An approximation formula for the minimal Coulomb energy E(n), explicit, fitted to 453 known putative optima; the object is a formula, not a configuration.

events.what_happened: Lai, Hao, Xiao and Fu, 'Global optimization and structural analysis of Coulomb and logarithmic potentials on the unit sphere using a population-based heuristic approach', Expert Systems with Applications 238 (Part A), article 121704, March 2024. A population-based metaheuristic (two-phase local optimisation with early stopping, random perturbation, distance-based population update, population rebuilding) is applied to Coulomb and discrete logarithmic energies on S² for N up to 500. The authors' GitHub repository (XiangjingLai/minimum-energy-configurations) cites the paper and says it contains 'the best solutions found for the tested instances'. A search excerpt says the algorithm improves the best-known Coulomb energy for N=360. I could not read the paper text: the author-hosted PDF returns a binary that the fetch tool cannot parse, so the N=360 figure and the new value are unverified.
events.revisions: Journal issue March 2024 (per the author's PDF citation and DBLP-style search excerpts). The online-first date was not found, so the first public date may be earlier than March 2024. The author-hosted PDF's metadata shows a 2021 file creation date, which is not a publication date.
events.delivers: If the N=360 claim holds: an improved upper bound on the minimal Coulomb energy for one instance (N=360). Also heuristic candidate configurations for the other tested N up to 500. Upper bounds only; no optimality certificate. It settles no value of N.
events.remains: Exact minimisers for every N; a heuristic upper bound cannot certify global minimality, and the N=360 value is not known to be final.

events.directly_checkable: The best configurations are said to be in the authors' GitHub repository; anyone can compute the Coulomb energy of a posted configuration and compare it with the Cambridge Cluster Database value. I did not check either.
events.doubts: Heuristic result with no optimality certificate. The N=360 claim rests on a search excerpt that I could not confirm in the paper text. The GitHub README contains no table of records and no N=360 value. The Amore et al. 2025 introduction describes this work as 'obtaining encouraging results' (arXiv 2506.08398, Section 1), not as a settlement.

events.object: Claimed lowest-found Coulomb configuration for N=360; the energy value and point coordinates were not retrieved. Numerical point sets (heuristic output), not an explicit construction; the set is said to be in the authors' repository.

events.what_happened: Amore and Sáenz, 'Lower and upper bounds for configurations of points on a sphere' (arXiv:2412.05800, v1 8 Dec 2024). A spectral-decomposition proof of a bound due to Sidelnikov for frame potentials on the sphere, extended to weighted sums, plus a sharp upper bound for a triple-sum expression in three dimensions. The Thomson problem appears only as an application: local minima at N=972 are examined, with no energy values or bounds reported for any N.
events.delivers: Nothing about the minimal Coulomb configuration or energy for any N. Frame-potential bounds are a different quantity.
events.direction: No direction on the Thomson problem; the frame-potential bound is a different question.

events.what_happened: Amore, Figueroa, Diaz, López and Vincent, 'Exploring the energy landscape of the Thomson problem: local minima and stationary states' (arXiv:2506.08398, submitted 10 Jun 2025). The paper counts local minima and stationary states for Coulomb configurations up to N=150 and reports that the number of distinct configurations grows exponentially, faster than previously reported (N≤24 for stationary states). It claims no new global minimum or improved energy.
events.delivers: Growth rates of local minima and stationary states for the Coulomb energy. No minimal energy configuration for any N.
events.direction: No direction on the minimiser; it is a landscape count.

events.what_happened: Amore, 'Thomson problem on a spherical cap' (arXiv:2508.17625, v1 25 Aug 2025; v2 4 Sep 2025). Low-energy Coulomb configurations on a spherical cap rather than the full sphere, with a numerical energy-minimisation method and an analysis of defects against N and cap curvature.
events.delivers: Nothing on the full-sphere problem. It answers a different question (a cap, not S²).
events.direction: Not about the full-sphere minimiser.

events.what_happened: Amore, Figueroa and Ramos, 'Exploring the energy landscape of the logarithmic potential: local minima and stationary states' (arXiv:2512.12416, submitted 13 Dec 2025). Landscape of the logarithmic potential on the sphere, local minima up to N=160, with the Coulomb case mentioned only as a comparison.
events.delivers: Nothing on the Coulomb problem: it addresses the logarithmic potential, the Smale-type energy rather than the Thomson one.
events.direction: Not about the Coulomb minimiser.

events.what_happened: Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao and Wagner, 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale' (arXiv:2511.02864, v1 3 Nov 2025), Section 18 'The Thomson and Tammes problems' (Problem 6.33). AlphaEvolve searched for point positions minimising the Coulomb energy for N up to 300 in the main runs (N < 50 matched the literature within the first hour; larger N about ten hours), and evolved generalising programs averaged over N = 4 to 500. Table 4 compares the literature benchmark with AlphaEvolve for N = 5, 10, 282, 292, 306; the values agree to about 10⁻⁸ or better. The paper says AlphaEvolve matched the state-of-the-art numerics rather than improving them. Whether Section 18 appears in v1 was not verified (the v1 date is the arXiv submission date).
events.revisions: v3 exists (html v3 read); v1 submission 3 Nov 2025.
events.delivers: Reproduces existing Coulomb records for N = 5, 10, 282, 292, 306 (and generally for N < 50) to high precision. No improvement; no exact result; the paper calls the work on lower-order asymptotic terms work in progress.
events.remains: Every exact minimiser for every n.
events.directly_checkable: The tabulated configurations are numerical; the energies can be recomputed from coordinates if the paper's data are released (not checked).
events.doubts: The results match records already in the literature; the paper does not claim a new Thomson record. The authors include Tao, Gómez-Serrano, Georgiev and Wagner, who are authors of this paper and therefore not independent checkers.
events.direction: Replicates the known minima numerically; does not cut against or for any conjecture beyond the numerical agreement.
events.object: Numerical point sets for N = 5, 10, 282, 292, 306 found by AlphaEvolve and matching the literature energies (for example N=306: 43862.569780796766 against a benchmark of 43862.569780797); numerical, not explicit, and not new.

systems.name: AlphaEvolve
systems.what_it_did: Evolutionary coding agent that searched point configurations minimising the Coulomb energy (main runs up to N=300) and evolved programs for a generalised energy average over N = 4 to 500. The results match the literature (Table 4); they are not improvements.
systems.basis_quote: matching the state of the art numerics to high precision.

events.what_happened: Bianchi, Kwon, Pappu and Zou, 'Harnessing the Collective Intelligence of AI Agents in the Wild for New Discoveries' (arXiv:2606.10402, submitted 9 Jun 2026; the EinsteinArena platform launched 19 March 2026). Appendix A.15 poses the Coulomb energy problem for 282 points on S² as a platform task. The best known value listed is 37147.29442, attributed to AlphaEvolve. The agents' column in Table 1 is empty ('-'), and Thomson is not among the 11 problems where the paper reports new state-of-the-art results. The paper reports no agent value.
events.delivers: Nothing: no agent value for N=282 is reported, so no bound moved.
events.remains: Everything in problem_asks, including the N=282 value.
events.direction: No result; no direction.

events.what_happened: Kryvonos, Liehr and Taylor, 'Energy minimization for eight points on the sphere' (arXiv:2609.22077, v1 submitted 18 Sep 2026). Theorem 1.1 (s ∈ {0, 1}, which includes the Coulomb case s=1) states that for every eight-point configuration Y, E_s(Y) ≥ E_s(X(a_s)), with equality iff Y is congruent to the square antiprism X(a_s). The Coulomb height parameter is a₁ ≈ 0.3140893678 with minimum energy ≈ 19.6752878612, the square antiprism with half-height √a₁. The height is the unique root in (0,1) of a stationarity equation F(s,a)=0 printed in the paper. The abstract calls the proof 'computer-assisted and fully verified in Lean'. The paper also states Theorem 1.2 (Riesz s above a threshold S, Lean-verified and not computer-assisted) and a computer-assisted proof for all s ≥ 0 (Remark 7.2), and gives completely monotone potentials for which the square antiprism is not the minimiser, answering a universality question of Cohn and Woo in the negative. The authors' §1.4 credits the main ideas to GPT-6 Astra (see ai).
events.revisions: v1 18 Sep 2026; no later version listed on the abstract page when checked (13 Oct 2026).
events.delivers: Settles N=8 for the Coulomb energy: the square antiprism is the unique global minimiser up to congruence, by a computer-assisted argument with Lean verification of the certificates. Also covers logarithmic energy at N=8 (s=0) and Riesz energies (s ≥ 0 by computer assistance; large s Lean-verified without computer assistance). Restricted to N=8.
events.remains: Every N other than 8, including N=9, 10, 11 and beyond, and the general all-n question.
events.time_since_posted: about 25 days; no human reading found

machine_checked.system: Lean (version not stated in the portion of the paper I could read)
machine_checked.note: The abstract says 'fully verified in Lean'; the paper's §1.3 says the Lean verification is 'one of the main novelties'. Whether any placeholder uses sorry was not established: the companion repository is cited as [8] but its URL was not retrieved, and §9 was not readable.

events.directly_checkable: The stationarity equation with s=1 (q = 3/2) and the coordinates of the square antiprism can be checked by hand; the printed energy 19.6752878612 matches the Wikipedia table value 19.675287861 for N=8 (D4d square antiprism).
events.doubts: Not yet read by any named human. The PDF was unreadable, so the GPT-6 Astra sentence was taken from the HTML render and not checked against the PDF. The companion repository (certificates and Lean development) was not retrieved. The Tooby-Smith and Zughaid README says its N=8 solution was found by Claude models after 'Claude had produced a full solution' and was posted only after this paper, which conflicts with the authors' attribution of the main ideas to GPT-6 Astra (see disputes). The paper's text is somewhat garbled in places (for example a figure printed as '9999 percent'); this does not touch the statements I read.
events.direction: Confirms the expected N=8 minimiser (the square antiprism, D4d), which is the numerically known one, and shows the Coulomb minimiser is unique up to congruence.
events.object: The square antiprism: two parallel squares of four points each, one rotated by 45 degrees relative to the other, with squared half-height a₁ ≈ 0.3140893678 (height √a₁) and Coulomb energy ≈ 19.6752878612. Explicit configuration; its optimality is established by a computer-assisted argument with Lean-verified numerical certificates, not by an existence proof.

systems.name: GPT-6 Astra
systems.what_it_did: Per the authors' §1.4 (Usage of Large Language Models), the main ideas in the proofs of Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 are due to this system. The authors' own role, per the same section, was to digest the proof, simplify the numerics and Lean-verify the numerical certificates.
systems.basis_quote: The main ideas in the proofs of Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 are due to GPT-6 Astra.

events.what_happened: Joseph Tooby-Smith and Alex Zughaid published a Lean development titled as a 'warrant' (GitHub jstoobysmith/Thomson-N-8-Warrant), with an edit line dated 25/09/26. The README says it gives a formal check that the N=8 Thomson problem is uniquely solved by the square antiprism at a set height, and that the authors 'do not call this a proof, but instead a warrant'. It says the result 'was found using Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 with a Claude Max subscription', that human prompting was 'minimal and only related to technicalities in Lean', and that the work was posted on arXiv (2609.22077) 'before we made this code public, but after Claude had produced a full solution'. It also says the N=7 case 'was followed trivially from similar techniques'. Files listed: Challenge.lean, Solution.lean, Thomson8.lean. The README gives no theorem statement.
events.revisions: README edit line 25/09/26; the first public date of the repository was not established. The README says the code was made public after 18 Sep 2026.
events.delivers: Per the README: a Lean check that the square antiprism is the unique minimiser of the N=8 Coulomb problem at a set height. The authors do not claim a proof, and the formal statement is not reproduced in the README. Restricted to N=8.
events.remains: Every N other than 8; the N=7 remark is an informal claim with no artefact in the repository I read.

machine_checked.system: Lean (version not stated in the README; a lean-toolchain file exists but its contents were not shown)

They call it a warrant, not a proof, and say it is 'very much a work in progress'. The sorry status and the Lean statement are not in the README. Its attribution of the N=8 solution to Claude models conflicts with the arXiv paper's attribution of the main ideas to GPT-6 Astra (see disputes).

events.object: The square antiprism at a fixed height, as the Lean target; explicit configuration.

events.what_happened: Hung Tran of Vals AI posted a Lean 4 proof (GitHub huwngtran/thomson-n7-lean, README 'Snapshot of 2026-09-27'; company blog 'A Lean Proof of the Thomson Problem for Seven Electrons' dated 09/28/2026) that the regular pentagonal bipyramid is the unique minimiser, up to rotation, reflection and relabelling, of the Coulomb energy for 7 points on S², with minimal energy 14.4529774142. Solution.lean is 17,895 lines and proves the fixed statements thomson_seven (global optimality) and thomson_seven_unique (uniqueness). The blog says ten Claude Sonnet 5.5 agents produced the proof over about 15 hours at maximum effort, with a message board, 1,270 messages and one agent acting as integrator; humans supplied two Lean theorem statements and nine suggested directions. A fork exists (narinluangrath/thomson-n7-lean, which says 'forked from huwngtran/thomson-n7-lean'). The Vals AI X post (not opened) was reshared on X.
events.revisions: README snapshot 2026-09-27; company blog 2026-09-28 (both are dated sources; the public-visibility date of the repository was not established); fork narinluangrath/thomson-n7-lean (snapshot 2026-09-27, one commit, no dates).
events.delivers: Claims the pentagonal bipyramid is the unique Coulomb minimiser for N=7 points on S², formally, in the form of the two fixed statements. The repository says the 'Statement not human-certified. Not peer reviewed.' Restricted to N=7.
events.remains: Every N other than 7, and the general all-n question. The faithfulness of the fixed Lean statements to the physical problem has not been checked by any named expert.
events.time_since_posted: about 16 days; no named mathematician response found

machine_checked.system: Lean 4.34.1 with Mathlib commit d13f23b723b8a846827a245b89c10fc7d3f11612; Lean Comparator ('Your solution is okay!', 260 s); second kernel nanoda (47,854 declarations accepted; a single changed certificate integer made it reject)
machine_checked.note: Sorry-freedom is reported through the '#print axioms' output (propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only), not run by me. The fixed challenge file ComparatorChallenges/ThomsonN7.lean has its theorems left as sorry by design.

events.directly_checkable: The pentagonal bipyramid (five equatorial points at 72 degrees and two poles) has energy 14.452977414 (Wikipedia table, D5h), checkable by hand. The fixed statements in the repository can be compared with the Coulomb energy definition.
events.doubts: (1) The repository itself says 'Statement not human-certified. Not peer reviewed.' (2) Startup Fortune and the Vocal piece both argue that Lean's kernel only confirms the formal statements; whether they match the physical problem is the key link, and I found no named expert review of them. (3) Human role is disputed: Vals says 'No human intervention, no preset division of labor'; the Vocal critique says humans wrote the two Lean statements, gave nine directions and set the success criteria, and that 'There was human upfront design'. A human mathematician is said to have opened the file (unnamed, search excerpt of the Vocal piece). (4) The method follows the N=8 work of Kryvonos, Liehr and Taylor (GPT-6 Astra credited) and the Lean development of Tooby-Smith and Zughaid (Claude credited). (5) The proof uses numerical SDP solvers whose outputs are rounded to exact certificates; Lean checks the certificates, so the numerics are not trusted, but the design is human and AI.
events.direction: Confirms the conjectured N=7 minimiser (the pentagonal bipyramid) and claims its uniqueness.
events.object: The regular pentagonal bipyramid (D5h): two poles and five equatorial points at 72-degree spacing, energy 14.4529774142. Explicit configuration; the claimed proof is an optimality and uniqueness argument with exact rational certificates checked in Lean, not an existence proof.

The humans supplied two Lean statements and nine directions, per the blog.
systems.basis_quote: I deployed ten Claude Sonnet 5.5 agents at maximum effort

ai.disclosed_cost: About 15 hours of agent time and 1,270 messages; no tokens or cost reported.

events.what_happened: Aravind Karthigeyan (listed on Zenodo as University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) published 'The Nine-Point Coulomb Thomson Problem: Lean Proof and Certificates', release v0.1.0 (GitHub aravindkarthigeyan/thomson-n9-lean; Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23192843). It claims a Lean 4 proof of global optimality and uniqueness, for 9 points on S² with the Coulomb (inverse-distance) energy, of the D3h tricapped trigonal prism (the triaugmented triangular prism in Wikipedia's table), with main theorem ThomsonN9.thomson_nine_complete. The release says 'External review requested' and 'not a claim of completed peer review or priority'. Its attribution note, dated 6 Oct 2026, says 'The work was AI-generated through Claude Opus 5.5 and Codex using GPT-6 Astra with Ultra reasoning effort, with additional imported Astra Pro artifacts', and that the human 'directed and published the project but does not claim to have written the proof or manuscript'. v0.1.1 is an attribution-only correction naming Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and GPT-6 Astra via Codex (gpt-6-astra, ultra).

disputes.summary: Conflicting AI credit for the N=8 solution. Kryvonos, Liehr and Taylor (arXiv:2609.22077, 18 Sep 2026, §1.4) say the main ideas of Theorems 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3 are due to GPT-6 Astra. Tooby-Smith and Zughaid (README edited 25/09/26) say the result was found using Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5, and that Claude had produced a full solution before their code was public. Both groups claim the square antiprism is the N=8 minimiser. No source I read reconciles the two accounts.

Order and provenance of the two N=8 Lean efforts. The arXiv paper was posted 18 Sep 2026; the Tooby-Smith README says its code was made public after that paper. The N=7 repository and blog build on the Kryvonos et al. method and cite the Tooby-Smith and Zughaid Lean development. The earliest date I could see for the Tooby-Smith code is its README edit of 25/09/26. Who first had a Lean-checked N=8 argument is not settled by the sources I read.

Human role in the N=7 proof. Vals AI's blog and its X post describe 'No human intervention, no preset division of labor' (as quoted in the Vocal critique), and the blog describes ten agents at maximum effort. The Vocal critique says humans wrote the two Lean theorem statements, supplied nine directions and set the success criteria ('There was human upfront design'). The blog itself describes the nine directions and the two statements.

Authorship changed on the N=9 release. The v0.1.0 release named Aravind Karthigeyan as author of the proof and manuscript. The attribution correction dated 6 Oct 2026 (v0.1.1) supersedes the human byline and credits Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra via Codex. The Zenodo record keeps Karthigeyan as listed creator and depositor 'at his request', with AI disclosed in the description. The repository says arXiv and Zenodo policies do not allow AI authors and that host clarification may be needed.

How hard the N=7 case is. The Tooby-Smith and Zughaid README says 'the N = 7 case was followed trivially from similar techniques'. The Vals blog presents the N=7 proof as a 15-hour agent effort that is a substantial step beyond the N=8 method. The two accounts disagree on the difficulty; neither gives an independent assessment.

summary: The bullet asks for the minimiser for each n, and no source gives a general answer, so the all-n question is unchanged; what has moved is the status of individual values. Three values have new claims in September and October 2026, all Lean-based and all crediting AI systems. N=8: Kryvonos, Liehr and Taylor (arXiv 2609.22077, 18 Sep 2026) prove, computer-assisted and Lean-verified, that the square antiprism is the unique Coulomb minimiser; their §1.4 credits GPT-6 Astra with the main ideas. Tooby-Smith and Zughaid (GitHub, edited 25 Sep 2026) give a Lean 'warrant' for the same statement and credit Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5, which contradicts the arXiv attribution. N=7: Hung Tran of Vals AI posted a 17,895-line Lean file (repository snapshot 27 Sep 2026; blog 28 Sep 2026) that the pentagonal bipyramid is the unique minimiser, which the authors say ten Claude Sonnet 5.5 agents produced; the repository says 'Statement not human-certified. Not peer reviewed.' Wikipedia's Thomson article (fetched October 2026) reports this as a claimed exact proof, and its exact-solutions list has not been updated for the N=8 arXiv paper. N=9: Aravind Karthigeyan's v0.1.0 release (6 Oct 2026, same date on Zenodo) claims a Lean proof for the tricapped (triaugmented) trigonal prism, AI-generated by Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra via Codex, with 'External review requested'; the authorship was changed to these systems in a correction dated the same day. I could not build or run any of the three Lean projects, and I checked the sorry status only from the authors' stated axiom lists. Before the window, Schwartz's computer-assisted N=5 proof (arXiv posted 21 Jan 2010; Experimental Mathematics 2013 per the author's site) settles N=5, and the classical N=4, 6, 12 optimality (Yudin, 1992) is reported only in secondary excerpts I could not verify in an opened source. Within the window, a 2024 population-based heuristic (Lai, Hao, Xiao, Fu; Expert Systems with Applications, March 2024) is reported by a search excerpt to improve the best-known Coulomb energy at N=360; the full text was unreadable to me, so that figure is unverified. Other 2025-2026 items are discounted: AlphaEvolve reproduced existing Coulomb records (3 Nov 2025) without improvement; the EinsteinArena attempt at N=282 reports no agent value; Amore et al. (2025) count local minima on the full sphere without a new minimum; and the spherical cap, logarithmic-potential and disk papers (2025-2026) answer different questions. Close calls: whether a single-n settlement counts against an all-n question (I record it as an event and leave the weighing to the judging pass); whether the Lean statements in the N=7 and N=9 repositories match the physical problem (no named expert has checked them); the first public date of the N=7 proof (27 Sep from the repository snapshot or 28 Sep from the blog) and of the N=9 release (6 Oct, with the original v0.1.0 posting not established); and the AI attribution for N=8, which two papers contradict. The AI record across the 2026 claims names GPT-6 Astra (N=8 main ideas, arXiv), Claude Fable 5.1 and Opus 5 (N=8 warrant), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (N=7), and Claude Opus 5.5 with GPT-6 Astra via Codex and Astra Pro artifacts (N=9). The 2025 AlphaEvolve work involved AI but its numerics match the literature, and the 2023 Moscato et al. paper used symbolic-regression tools (Eureqa, TuringBot) only for approximation formulas.
competing_reading: Nothing has been settled in the sense the bullet asks. The bullet is about every n, and N=7, N=8 and N=9 are three instances; by the scope rule for universal claims (the 1-3-2-3 and Collatz cases in §2.1), finitely many instances of a question about all n move nothing that the question names. On that reading the status is 'open' with three new instance-level events, none changing the general answer. Against that, each n is a separate question the bullet names, so settling a value of n is a change to what the entry should say; and three exact values were, until 2026, known only numerically. Both readings rest on the same facts recorded above.
what_would_settle_it: (1) An expert check that the Lean statements (the fixed challenge file ComparatorChallenges/ThomsonN7.lean in the N=7 repository, and the challenge statements in the N=8 and N=9 repositories) match the Coulomb energy on S² with distinct points, and a build of each project. (2) The full text of arXiv 2609.22077 (the PDF was unreadable to me, and §9 and the companion repository were not retrieved), including whether any placeholder uses sorry and what the acknowledgements say, and a reconciliation of its GPT-6 Astra credit with the Tooby-Smith and Zughaid Claude credit. (3) The Expert Systems with Applications 2024 full text, or the Cambridge Cluster Database entry for N=360, to confirm or reject the Lai et al. improvement. (4) An external review of the N=9 release (requested in the repository). (5) The abstract and content of Discrete Applied Mathematics article S0166218X26002982 (a 2026 paper on deterministic global optimisation for the Thomson and Tammes problems; ScienceDirect returned 403, so I could not read it). (6) For the all-n reading, any result giving minimisers for a family of n, which none of the sources show.

event.what_happened: Kryvonos, Liehr and Taylor, 'Energy minimization for eight points on the sphere' (arXiv:2609.22077, v1 submitted 18 Sep 2026). Theorem 1.1 (s ∈ {0, 1}, which includes the Coulomb case s=1) states that for every eight-point configuration Y, E_s(Y) ≥ E_s(X(a_s)), with equality iff Y is congruent to the square antiprism X(a_s). The Coulomb height parameter is a₁ ≈ 0.3140893678 with minimum energy ≈ 19.6752878612, the square antiprism with half-height √a₁. The height is the unique root in (0,1) of a stationarity equation F(s,a)=0 printed in the paper. The abstract calls the proof 'computer-assisted and fully verified in Lean'. The paper also states Theorem 1.2 (Riesz s above a threshold S, Lean-verified and not computer-assisted) and a computer-assisted proof for all s ≥ 0 (Remark 7.2), and gives completely monotone potentials for which the square antiprism is not the minimiser, answering a universality question of Cohn and Woo in the negative. The authors' §1.4 credits the main ideas to GPT-6 Astra (see ai).
event.revisions: v1 18 Sep 2026; no later version listed on the abstract page when checked (13 Oct 2026).
event.delivers: Settles N=8 for the Coulomb energy: the square antiprism is the unique global minimiser up to congruence, by a computer-assisted argument with Lean verification of the certificates. Also covers logarithmic energy at N=8 (s=0) and Riesz energies (s ≥ 0 by computer assistance; large s Lean-verified without computer assistance). Restricted to N=8.
event.remains: Every N other than 8, including N=9, 10, 11 and beyond, and the general all-n question.

event.directly_checkable: The stationarity equation with s=1 (q = 3/2) and the coordinates of the square antiprism can be checked by hand; the printed energy 19.6752878612 matches the Wikipedia table value 19.675287861 for N=8 (D4d square antiprism).
event.doubts: Not yet read by any named human. The PDF was unreadable, so the GPT-6 Astra sentence was taken from the HTML render and not checked against the PDF. The companion repository (certificates and Lean development) was not retrieved. The Tooby-Smith and Zughaid README says its N=8 solution was found by Claude models after 'Claude had produced a full solution' and was posted only after this paper, which conflicts with the authors' attribution of the main ideas to GPT-6 Astra (see disputes). The paper's text is somewhat garbled in places (for example a figure printed as '9999 percent'); this does not touch the statements I read.
event.direction: Confirms the expected N=8 minimiser (the square antiprism, D4d), which is the numerically known one, and shows the Coulomb minimiser is unique up to congruence.
event.object: The square antiprism: two parallel squares of four points each, one rotated by 45 degrees relative to the other, with squared half-height a₁ ≈ 0.3140893678 (height √a₁) and Coulomb energy ≈ 19.6752878612. Explicit configuration; its optimality is established by a computer-assisted argument with Lean-verified numerical certificates, not by an existence proof.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the minimiser for every n, so a proof for one n settles a restriction (case), not the whole; I rejected the researcher's 'instances' reading because each n's answer is a full infinite-configuration optimisation proof, not a finite check of a universal statement. The N=7, 8, 9 claims are Lean-checked but no named human has read any of them, so all are unreviewed (F7). All four credit AI with producing the mathematics in the authors' own words, so generated. AlphaEvolve only reproduced known numerics (none); disk, cap, logarithmic and Riesz-family work is variant. Lai 2024 is a one-instance upper bound, journal-published but resting on an unverified excerpt, so it is a doubtful bound; its March 2024 issue date is after the snapshot, though online-first may be earlier.
judgement.doubts: Case vs instances for single-n results is the main close call. Lai's verification is marked digested because of journal acceptance, but the N=360 claim itself was never seen. The N=8 AI attribution is disputed between GPT-6 Astra and Claude; each event is credited only from its own quote.
judgement.by: judging pass (JUDGE.md), claude-opus-5-5; not the researching agent and not a human reviewer
